The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a [gold funerary mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_masks_of_Mycenae "Death masks of Mycenae") which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the [National Archaeological Museum of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Athens "National Archaeological Museum of Athens"), has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_[Mona Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona\_Lisa "Mona Lisa")_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)

German archaeologist [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann"), who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon"), leader of the [Achaeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaeans_(Homer) "Achaeans (Homer)") in the ancient Greek epic of the [Trojan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War"), the _[Iliad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mask_of_Agamemnon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Discovery")]

Heinrich Schliemann found the gold [funeral mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_mask "Funeral mask") in 1876 in a [shaft tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_tomb "Shaft tomb") designated Grave V, at the site [Grave Circle A, Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_A,_Mycenae "Grave Circle A, Mycenae").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)

The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon") of Homer's _[Iliad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")_. Schliemann took this as evidence the [Trojan War was a real historical event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicity_of_the_Trojan_War "Historicity of the Trojan War").

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg/250px-Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg)

Portrait of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann")

The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details [chased](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repouss%C3%A9_and_chasing "Repoussé and chasing") on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified [King George I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Greece "George I of Greece").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named [his son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon_Schliemann "Agamemnon Schliemann") after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)

## Authenticity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mask_of_Agamemnon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Authenticity")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22%2C_NAMA_624%2C_225545.jpg/250px-Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22%2C_NAMA_624%2C_225545.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22,_NAMA_624,_225545.jpg)

The mask in the National Archaeological Museum

In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_[Archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology\_(magazine) "Archaeology (magazine)")_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the [Shaft Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_Graves "Shaft Graves"), the [Greek Archaeological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Archaeological_Society "Greek Archaeological Society") had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy")), sending [Panagiotis Stamatakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panagiotis_Stamatakis "Panagiotis Stamatakis") as _[ephor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephor\_(archaeology) "Ephor (archaeology)")_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.

Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.

The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.

A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in [Mycenaean art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_art "Mycenaean art") has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.

The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head [rhyton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyton "Rhyton") from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a [vendetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feud "Feud").

Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a [gold funerary mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_masks_of_Mycenae "Death masks of Mycenae") which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the [National Archaeological Museum of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum_of_Athens "National Archaeological Museum of Athens"), has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_[Mona Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona\_Lisa "Mona Lisa")_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)

German archaeologist [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann"), who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon"), leader of the [Achaeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaeans_(Homer) "Achaeans (Homer)") in the ancient Greek epic of the [Trojan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War"), the _[Iliad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mask_of_Agamemnon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Discovery")]

Heinrich Schliemann found the gold [funeral mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_mask "Funeral mask") in 1876 in a [shaft tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_tomb "Shaft tomb") designated Grave V, at the site [Grave Circle A, Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_A,_Mycenae "Grave Circle A, Mycenae").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)

The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon") of Homer's _[Iliad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")_. Schliemann took this as evidence the [Trojan War was a real historical event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicity_of_the_Trojan_War "Historicity of the Trojan War").

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg/250px-Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heinrich_Schliemann.jpg)

Portrait of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann")

The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details [chased](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repouss%C3%A9_and_chasing "Repoussé and chasing") on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified [King George I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Greece "George I of Greece").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named [his son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon_Schliemann "Agamemnon Schliemann") after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)

## Authenticity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mask_of_Agamemnon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Authenticity")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22%2C_NAMA_624%2C_225545.jpg/250px-Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22%2C_NAMA_624%2C_225545.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Funeral_mask_Mycenae_%22Agamemnon%22,_NAMA_624,_225545.jpg)

The mask in the National Archaeological Museum

In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_[Archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology\_(magazine) "Archaeology (magazine)")_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the [Shaft Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaft_Graves "Shaft Graves"), the [Greek Archaeological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Archaeological_Society "Greek Archaeological Society") had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy")), sending [Panagiotis Stamatakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panagiotis_Stamatakis "Panagiotis Stamatakis") as _[ephor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephor\_(archaeology) "Ephor (archaeology)")_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.

Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.

The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.

A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in [Mycenaean art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_art "Mycenaean art") has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.

The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head [rhyton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyton "Rhyton") from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a [vendetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feud "Feud").

Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

The **National Archaeological Museum** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Εθνικό Αρχαιολογικό Μουσείο, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"):_Ethnikó Archaiologikó Mouseío_) in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") houses some of the most important artifacts from a variety of archaeological locations around [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") from [prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory "Prehistory") to [late antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_antiquity "Late antiquity"). It is considered one of the greatest museums in the world and contains the richest collection of Greek Antiquity artifacts worldwide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-1) It is situated in the [Exarcheia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exarcheia "Exarcheia") area in central Athens between Epirus Street, Bouboulinas Street and Tositsas Street while its entrance is on the [Patission Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patission_Street "Patission Street"), adjacent to the historical building of the [National Technical University of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Technical_University_of_Athens "National Technical University of Athens").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/National_Museum_6.jpg/330px-National_Museum_6.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:National_Museum_6.jpg)

The Museum in 1893

The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established by the governor of Greece, [Ioannis Kapodistrias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioannis_Kapodistrias "Ioannis Kapodistrias"), in [Aigina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aigina "Aigina") in 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum's building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889, using funds from the [Greek Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Government "Greek Government"), the [Greek Archaeological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Archaeological_Society "Greek Archaeological Society") and the society of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae"). Major benefactors were [Eleni Tositsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleni_Tositsa "Eleni Tositsa") who donated the land for the building of the museum, and Demetrios and Nikolaos [Vernardakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernardakis?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vernardakis (page does not exist)") from [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg"), who donated a large amount for the completion of the museum.

The initial name for the museum was _The Central Museum_. It was renamed to its current name in 1881 by the [Prime Minister of Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Greece "Prime Minister of Greece"), [Charilaos Trikoupis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charilaos_Trikoupis "Charilaos Trikoupis"). In 1887, the archaeologist [Valerios Stais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerios_Stais "Valerios Stais") became the museum's curator.

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. In 1945, exhibits were again displayed under the direction of [Christos Karouzos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Karouzos "Christos Karouzos") and [Semni Karouzou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semni_Karouzou "Semni Karouzou"). The south wing of the museum houses the [Epigraphical Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigraphical_Museum "Epigraphical Museum") with the richest collection of inscriptions in the world. The inscriptions museum expanded between 1953 and 1960, with the architectural designs of [Patroklos Karantinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patroklos_Karantinos "Patroklos Karantinos").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-3)

## The building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The building")]

The museum has an imposing [neo-classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") design which was very popular in Europe at the time and is in accordance with the [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classicism "Classicism") style artifacts that it houses. The initial plan was conceived by the architect [Ludwig Lange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Lange_(architect) "Ludwig Lange (architect)") and it was later modified by [Panagis Kalkos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panagis_Kalkos "Panagis Kalkos") who was the main architect, [Armodios Vlachos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armodios_Vlachos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Armodios Vlachos (page does not exist)") and [Ernst Ziller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Ziller "Ernst Ziller"). At the front of the museum there is a large [neo-classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassicism "Neoclassicism") design garden which is decorated with sculptures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

## Expansions and renovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansions and renovations")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/0028MAN-Room3.jpg/250px-0028MAN-Room3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:0028MAN-Room3.jpg)

The [Antikythera Ephebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")

The building has undergone many expansions. Most important were the construction of a new east wing in the early 20th century, based on the plans of [Anastasios Metaxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasios_Metaxas "Anastasios Metaxas") and the construction of a two-storeyed building, designed by [George Nomikos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nomikos?action=edit&redlink=1 "George Nomikos (page does not exist)"), during 1932–1939.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2) These expansions were necessary to accommodate the rapidly growing collection of artifacts. The most recent refurbishment of the museum took more than 1.5 years to complete, during which the museum remained completely closed. It reopened in July 2004, in time for the [Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") and it included an aesthetic and technical upgrade of the building, installation of a modern air-conditioning system, reorganisation of the museum's collection and repair of the damage caused by the 1999 [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake"). The Minoan frescoes rooms opened to the public in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-4) In May 2008, the Culture Minister, Mihalis Liapis, inaugurated the much anticipated collection of Egyptian antiquities and the collection of Eleni and Antonis Stathatos.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-5)

In 2020, there was renewed discussion regarding the need to further expand the museum to adjacent areas. A new plan was made for a subterranean expansion at the front of the museum.

In 2023, the Greek government approved plans for a 20,000 square metre underground extension to the museum. The extension is expected to be completed by 2028 and will also feature a rooftop garden.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-6)

### Prehistoric collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Prehistoric collection")]

The prehistoric collection displays objects from the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") era (6800–3000 BC), Early and Mid-[Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") (3000–2000 BC and 2000 to 1700 BC respectively), objects classified as [Cycladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycladic "Cycladic") and [Mycenaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic_period "Helladic period") art.

#### Neolithic era and early and mid-Bronze Age collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Neolithic era and early and mid-Bronze Age collection")]

There are ceramic finds from various important Neolithic sites, such as [Dimini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimini "Dimini") and [Sesclo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesclo "Sesclo"), and from middle [Helladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic "Helladic") ceramics from [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia "Boeotia"), [Attica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attica "Attica") and [Phthiotis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phthiotis "Phthiotis"). Some objects from [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") excavations in [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy") are also on display. #### Cycladic art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Cycladic art collection")]

#### Mycenean art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mycenean art collection")]

Mycenean civilization is represented by stone, bronze and ceramic pots, figurines, ivory, glass and faience objects, golden [seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_(insignia) "Seal (insignia)") and rings from the vaulted tombs in Mycenae and other locations in the Peloponnese ([Tiryns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiryns "Tiryns") and [Dendra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendra "Dendra") in [Argolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argolis "Argolis"), [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") in [Messinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinia "Messinia") and [Vaphio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaphio "Vaphio") in [Lakonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakonia "Lakonia")). Of great interest are the two golden cups from Vafeio showing a scene of the capture of a bull.

#### Heinrich Schliemann finds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Heinrich Schliemann finds")]

Mycenean collection includes also the magnificent 19th-century finds of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") in [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") from the [Grave Circle A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_A,_Mycenae "Grave Circle A, Mycenae") and the earlier [Grave Circle B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_B,_Mycenae "Grave Circle B, Mycenae"). Most notable are the golden funerary masks which covered the faces of deceased Mycenean nobles. Among them, the most famous is the one that was named erroneously as the mask of Agamemnon. There are also finds from the citadel of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") including relief stelae, golden containers, glass, alabaster and amber tools and jewels. Other features include an ivory carving of two goddesses with a child, a painted limestone head of a goddess and the famous warrior's vase dating from the 12th century.

### Egyptian art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Egyptian art collection")]

The [Egyptian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt") collection dates back to the last twenty years of the 19th century. Notable is the donation of the Egyptian government which in 1893 offered nine mummies of the era of the [Pharaohs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharaoh "Pharaoh") from [Bab el-Gasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_el-Gasus "Bab el-Gasus"). However, the Egyptian collection is mainly by two donors, [Ioannis Dimitriou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioannis_Dimitriou "Ioannis Dimitriou") (in 1880) and of Alexandros Rostovic (in 1904). In total, the collection includes more than 6000 artefacts, 1100 of which are available presently for the public. The collection is considered to be one of the best collections of [Egyptian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_ancient_Egypt "Art of ancient Egypt") in the world.

The exhibition features rare statues, tools, jewels, mummies, a wooden body tag for a mummy, a bronze statue of a princess, intact bird eggs and a 3000-year-old loaf of bread with a bite-sized chunk missing. The exhibition centrepiece is a bronze statue of the princess-priestess [Takushit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takushit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Takushit (page does not exist)"), dating to around 670 BC. Standing 70 cm high and wearing a gown covered in hieroglyphs, the statue was found south of [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria") in 1880.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-12)

### Stathatos collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Stathatos collection")]

The Stathatos collection is named for the donors and major Greek benefactors Antonis and Eleni Stathatos. The collection features about 1000 objects, mainly jewels as well as metal objects, vases, and pottery from the Middle [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") to post-[Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine") era. Features of special note are the [Hellenistic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_period "Hellenistic period") golden jewels from [Karpenissi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karpenissi "Karpenissi") and [Thessaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaly "Thessaly").

## Artists and artifacts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Artists and artifacts")]

Some of the ancient artists whose work is presented in the museum are [Myron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myron "Myron"), [Scopas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopas "Scopas"), [Euthymides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthymides "Euthymides"), [Lydos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydos "Lydos"), [Agoracritus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoracritus "Agoracritus"), [Agasias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agasias,_son_of_Menophilus "Agasias, son of Menophilus"), [Pan Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Painter "Pan Painter"), [Wedding Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_Painter "Wedding Painter"), [Meleager Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meleager_Painter "Meleager Painter"), [Cimon of Cleonae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimon_of_Cleonae "Cimon of Cleonae"), [Nessos Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessos_Painter "Nessos Painter"), [Damophon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damophon "Damophon"), [Aison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aison_(vase_painter) "Aison (vase painter)"), [Analatos Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analatos_Painter "Analatos Painter"), [Polygnotos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygnotos_(vase_painter) "Polygnotos (vase painter)"), and [Hermonax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermonax "Hermonax").

Collections include [sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") work, [Loutrophoros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loutrophoros "Loutrophoros"), [amphora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphora "Amphora"), [Hydria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydria "Hydria"), [Skyphos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyphos "Skyphos"), [Krater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krater "Krater"), [Pelike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelike "Pelike"), and [lekythos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lekythos "Lekythos") vessels, [stele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stele "Stele"), [frescoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresco "Fresco"), jewellery, weapons, tools, coins, toys and other ancient items.

Artifacts derive from archaeological excavations in [Santorini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini "Santorini"), [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae"), [Tiryns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiryns "Tiryns"), [Dodona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodona "Dodona"), [Vaphio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaphio "Vaphio"), [Rhamnous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhamnous "Rhamnous"), [Lycosura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycosura "Lycosura"), [Aegean islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_islands "Aegean islands"), [Delos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delos "Delos"), the [Temple of Aphaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Aphaea "Temple of Aphaea") in [Aegina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegina "Aegina"), the [Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary_of_Artemis_Orthia "Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia") in [Sparta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta "Sparta"), [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pylos "Pylos"), [Thebes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thebes,_Greece "Thebes, Greece"), Athens, [Vari Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vari_Cave "Vari Cave"), the [Antikythera wreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_wreck "Antikythera wreck") and from various other places in [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

The museum houses the archaic terracota statuette [daidala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daidala "Daidala") that inspired the designers of the 2004 [Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") mascots, [Athena and Phevos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_and_Phevos "Athena and Phevos").

## Library of archaeology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Library of archaeology")]

The museum houses a 118-year-old library of archeology with rare ancient art, science and philosophy books and publications. The library has some 20,000 volumes, including rare editions dating to the 17th century.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-15) The bibliography covers archaeology, history, arts, [ancient Greek religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_religion "Ancient Greek religion") and [ancient Greek philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_philosophy "Ancient Greek philosophy"), as well as Ancient Greek and Latin literature. Of particular value are the diaries of various excavations including those of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann"). The collection of archaeology books is the richest of its kind in [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"). The Library has been recently renovated with funds from the [Alexander S. Onassis Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_S._Onassis_Foundation "Alexander S. Onassis Foundation"). Its renovation was completed on 26 May 2008 and is now named after [Alexander Onassis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Onassis "Alexander Onassis").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-16)

## Access

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Access")]

The museum is accessible by the [Athens Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens_Metro "Athens Metro"). The nearest station is Victoria Station (Line 1) and it is within a 5-minute walk from the museum. The museum houses a gift shop with artifact replicas and a café in the sculpture garden. The museum is fully wheelchair accessible. There are also facilities and guides for hearing-impaired visitors. It is next to the old building of the National Technical University and is served by bus, trolleybus and metro. It is not served by Proastiakos or the Athens Tram.

The **National Archaeological Museum** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Εθνικό Αρχαιολογικό Μουσείο, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"):_Ethnikó Archaiologikó Mouseío_) in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") houses some of the most important artifacts from a variety of archaeological locations around [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") from [prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory "Prehistory") to [late antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_antiquity "Late antiquity"). It is considered one of the greatest museums in the world and contains the richest collection of Greek Antiquity artifacts worldwide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-1) It is situated in the [Exarcheia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exarcheia "Exarcheia") area in central Athens between Epirus Street, Bouboulinas Street and Tositsas Street while its entrance is on the [Patission Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patission_Street "Patission Street"), adjacent to the historical building of the [National Technical University of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Technical_University_of_Athens "National Technical University of Athens").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/National_Museum_6.jpg/330px-National_Museum_6.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:National_Museum_6.jpg)

The Museum in 1893

The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established by the governor of Greece, [Ioannis Kapodistrias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioannis_Kapodistrias "Ioannis Kapodistrias"), in [Aigina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aigina "Aigina") in 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum's building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889, using funds from the [Greek Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Government "Greek Government"), the [Greek Archaeological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Archaeological_Society "Greek Archaeological Society") and the society of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae"). Major benefactors were [Eleni Tositsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleni_Tositsa "Eleni Tositsa") who donated the land for the building of the museum, and Demetrios and Nikolaos [Vernardakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernardakis?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vernardakis (page does not exist)") from [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg"), who donated a large amount for the completion of the museum.

The initial name for the museum was _The Central Museum_. It was renamed to its current name in 1881 by the [Prime Minister of Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Greece "Prime Minister of Greece"), [Charilaos Trikoupis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charilaos_Trikoupis "Charilaos Trikoupis"). In 1887, the archaeologist [Valerios Stais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerios_Stais "Valerios Stais") became the museum's curator.

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. In 1945, exhibits were again displayed under the direction of [Christos Karouzos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Karouzos "Christos Karouzos") and [Semni Karouzou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semni_Karouzou "Semni Karouzou"). The south wing of the museum houses the [Epigraphical Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigraphical_Museum "Epigraphical Museum") with the richest collection of inscriptions in the world. The inscriptions museum expanded between 1953 and 1960, with the architectural designs of [Patroklos Karantinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patroklos_Karantinos "Patroklos Karantinos").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-3)

## The building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The building")]

The museum has an imposing [neo-classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") design which was very popular in Europe at the time and is in accordance with the [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classicism "Classicism") style artifacts that it houses. The initial plan was conceived by the architect [Ludwig Lange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Lange_(architect) "Ludwig Lange (architect)") and it was later modified by [Panagis Kalkos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panagis_Kalkos "Panagis Kalkos") who was the main architect, [Armodios Vlachos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armodios_Vlachos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Armodios Vlachos (page does not exist)") and [Ernst Ziller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Ziller "Ernst Ziller"). At the front of the museum there is a large [neo-classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassicism "Neoclassicism") design garden which is decorated with sculptures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

## Expansions and renovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansions and renovations")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/0028MAN-Room3.jpg/250px-0028MAN-Room3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:0028MAN-Room3.jpg)

The [Antikythera Ephebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")

The building has undergone many expansions. Most important were the construction of a new east wing in the early 20th century, based on the plans of [Anastasios Metaxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasios_Metaxas "Anastasios Metaxas") and the construction of a two-storeyed building, designed by [George Nomikos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nomikos?action=edit&redlink=1 "George Nomikos (page does not exist)"), during 1932–1939.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2) These expansions were necessary to accommodate the rapidly growing collection of artifacts. The most recent refurbishment of the museum took more than 1.5 years to complete, during which the museum remained completely closed. It reopened in July 2004, in time for the [Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") and it included an aesthetic and technical upgrade of the building, installation of a modern air-conditioning system, reorganisation of the museum's collection and repair of the damage caused by the 1999 [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake"). The Minoan frescoes rooms opened to the public in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-4) In May 2008, the Culture Minister, Mihalis Liapis, inaugurated the much anticipated collection of Egyptian antiquities and the collection of Eleni and Antonis Stathatos.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-5)

In 2020, there was renewed discussion regarding the need to further expand the museum to adjacent areas. A new plan was made for a subterranean expansion at the front of the museum.

In 2023, the Greek government approved plans for a 20,000 square metre underground extension to the museum. The extension is expected to be completed by 2028 and will also feature a rooftop garden.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-6)

### Prehistoric collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Prehistoric collection")]

The prehistoric collection displays objects from the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") era (6800–3000 BC), Early and Mid-[Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") (3000–2000 BC and 2000 to 1700 BC respectively), objects classified as [Cycladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycladic "Cycladic") and [Mycenaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic_period "Helladic period") art.

#### Neolithic era and early and mid-Bronze Age collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Neolithic era and early and mid-Bronze Age collection")]

There are ceramic finds from various important Neolithic sites, such as [Dimini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimini "Dimini") and [Sesclo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesclo "Sesclo"), and from middle [Helladic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic "Helladic") ceramics from [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia "Boeotia"), [Attica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attica "Attica") and [Phthiotis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phthiotis "Phthiotis"). Some objects from [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") excavations in [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy") are also on display. #### Cycladic art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Cycladic art collection")]

#### Mycenean art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mycenean art collection")]

Mycenean civilization is represented by stone, bronze and ceramic pots, figurines, ivory, glass and faience objects, golden [seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_(insignia) "Seal (insignia)") and rings from the vaulted tombs in Mycenae and other locations in the Peloponnese ([Tiryns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiryns "Tiryns") and [Dendra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendra "Dendra") in [Argolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argolis "Argolis"), [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pylos "Pylos") in [Messinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinia "Messinia") and [Vaphio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaphio "Vaphio") in [Lakonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakonia "Lakonia")). Of great interest are the two golden cups from Vafeio showing a scene of the capture of a bull.

#### Heinrich Schliemann finds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Heinrich Schliemann finds")]

Mycenean collection includes also the magnificent 19th-century finds of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann") in [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") from the [Grave Circle A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_A,_Mycenae "Grave Circle A, Mycenae") and the earlier [Grave Circle B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave_Circle_B,_Mycenae "Grave Circle B, Mycenae"). Most notable are the golden funerary masks which covered the faces of deceased Mycenean nobles. Among them, the most famous is the one that was named erroneously as the mask of Agamemnon. There are also finds from the citadel of [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae") including relief stelae, golden containers, glass, alabaster and amber tools and jewels. Other features include an ivory carving of two goddesses with a child, a painted limestone head of a goddess and the famous warrior's vase dating from the 12th century.

### Egyptian art collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Egyptian art collection")]

The [Egyptian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt") collection dates back to the last twenty years of the 19th century. Notable is the donation of the Egyptian government which in 1893 offered nine mummies of the era of the [Pharaohs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharaoh "Pharaoh") from [Bab el-Gasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_el-Gasus "Bab el-Gasus"). However, the Egyptian collection is mainly by two donors, [Ioannis Dimitriou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioannis_Dimitriou "Ioannis Dimitriou") (in 1880) and of Alexandros Rostovic (in 1904). In total, the collection includes more than 6000 artefacts, 1100 of which are available presently for the public. The collection is considered to be one of the best collections of [Egyptian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_ancient_Egypt "Art of ancient Egypt") in the world.

The exhibition features rare statues, tools, jewels, mummies, a wooden body tag for a mummy, a bronze statue of a princess, intact bird eggs and a 3000-year-old loaf of bread with a bite-sized chunk missing. The exhibition centrepiece is a bronze statue of the princess-priestess [Takushit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takushit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Takushit (page does not exist)"), dating to around 670 BC. Standing 70 cm high and wearing a gown covered in hieroglyphs, the statue was found south of [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria") in 1880.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-12)

### Stathatos collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Stathatos collection")]

The Stathatos collection is named for the donors and major Greek benefactors Antonis and Eleni Stathatos. The collection features about 1000 objects, mainly jewels as well as metal objects, vases, and pottery from the Middle [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") to post-[Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine") era. Features of special note are the [Hellenistic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_period "Hellenistic period") golden jewels from [Karpenissi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karpenissi "Karpenissi") and [Thessaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaly "Thessaly").

## Artists and artifacts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Artists and artifacts")]

Some of the ancient artists whose work is presented in the museum are [Myron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myron "Myron"), [Scopas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopas "Scopas"), [Euthymides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthymides "Euthymides"), [Lydos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydos "Lydos"), [Agoracritus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoracritus "Agoracritus"), [Agasias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agasias,_son_of_Menophilus "Agasias, son of Menophilus"), [Pan Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Painter "Pan Painter"), [Wedding Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_Painter "Wedding Painter"), [Meleager Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meleager_Painter "Meleager Painter"), [Cimon of Cleonae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimon_of_Cleonae "Cimon of Cleonae"), [Nessos Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessos_Painter "Nessos Painter"), [Damophon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damophon "Damophon"), [Aison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aison_(vase_painter) "Aison (vase painter)"), [Analatos Painter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analatos_Painter "Analatos Painter"), [Polygnotos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygnotos_(vase_painter) "Polygnotos (vase painter)"), and [Hermonax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermonax "Hermonax").

Collections include [sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") work, [Loutrophoros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loutrophoros "Loutrophoros"), [amphora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphora "Amphora"), [Hydria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydria "Hydria"), [Skyphos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyphos "Skyphos"), [Krater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krater "Krater"), [Pelike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelike "Pelike"), and [lekythos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lekythos "Lekythos") vessels, [stele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stele "Stele"), [frescoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresco "Fresco"), jewellery, weapons, tools, coins, toys and other ancient items.

Artifacts derive from archaeological excavations in [Santorini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini "Santorini"), [Mycenae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae "Mycenae"), [Tiryns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiryns "Tiryns"), [Dodona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodona "Dodona"), [Vaphio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaphio "Vaphio"), [Rhamnous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhamnous "Rhamnous"), [Lycosura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycosura "Lycosura"), [Aegean islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_islands "Aegean islands"), [Delos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delos "Delos"), the [Temple of Aphaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Aphaea "Temple of Aphaea") in [Aegina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegina "Aegina"), the [Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary_of_Artemis_Orthia "Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia") in [Sparta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta "Sparta"), [Pylos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pylos "Pylos"), [Thebes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thebes,_Greece "Thebes, Greece"), Athens, [Vari Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vari_Cave "Vari Cave"), the [Antikythera wreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_wreck "Antikythera wreck") and from various other places in [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

The museum houses the archaic terracota statuette [daidala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daidala "Daidala") that inspired the designers of the 2004 [Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") mascots, [Athena and Phevos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_and_Phevos "Athena and Phevos").

## Library of archaeology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Library of archaeology")]

The museum houses a 118-year-old library of archeology with rare ancient art, science and philosophy books and publications. The library has some 20,000 volumes, including rare editions dating to the 17th century.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-15) The bibliography covers archaeology, history, arts, [ancient Greek religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_religion "Ancient Greek religion") and [ancient Greek philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_philosophy "Ancient Greek philosophy"), as well as Ancient Greek and Latin literature. Of particular value are the diaries of various excavations including those of [Heinrich Schliemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann"). The collection of archaeology books is the richest of its kind in [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"). The Library has been recently renovated with funds from the [Alexander S. Onassis Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_S._Onassis_Foundation "Alexander S. Onassis Foundation"). Its renovation was completed on 26 May 2008 and is now named after [Alexander Onassis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Onassis "Alexander Onassis").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-16)

## Access

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Access")]

The museum is accessible by the [Athens Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens_Metro "Athens Metro"). The nearest station is Victoria Station (Line 1) and it is within a 5-minute walk from the museum. The museum houses a gift shop with artifact replicas and a café in the sculpture garden. The museum is fully wheelchair accessible. There are also facilities and guides for hearing-impaired visitors. It is next to the old building of the National Technical University and is served by bus, trolleybus and metro. It is not served by Proastiakos or the Athens Tram.

# Greek Archaeological Treasures: The “Mask of Agamemnon”

[Duncan Howitt-Marshall](https://www.greece-is.com/author/dhmarshall/)|March 14th, 2022

![Image 4](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Mask-of-Agamemnon.jpg)

## When discovered at Mycenae in 1876, Schliemann famously exclaimed “I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon!” But did it really belong to the legendary king?

“I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon,” boasted **Heinrich Schliemann, the famous amateur archaeologist** who first unearthed the gold funeral mask at Mycenae in 1876.

Imagine his excitement and joy as he carefully brushed away the dirt to reveal the mask, depicting the face of a bearded man, glinting in the sunlight. But did it really belong to the king of Homeric legend?

Schliemann discovered the mask, still fastened to its corpse, in **Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A, immediately south of the Lion Gate**, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel in the Greek Argolid. It was one of seven death masks discovered in the same grave circle, alongside an enormous cache of gold artifacts, inlcuding ornate weapons, staffs, jewelry, and ceremonial cups.

Greek history books

Ever his own best publicist and exercising a blind faith in the Homeric epics, Schliemann made the extraordinary claim that he had found the remains of **Agamemnon, the legendary Mycenaean ruler**, in a telegraph to King George of Greece.

Agamemnon’s exploits as the commander-in-chief of the Greek army at Troy were immortalized in **Homer’s _Iliad_**. He was murdered upon his return from the war by Aegisthus, the lover of his wife Clytemnestra – the story of the Aeschylus’ tragic play “Agamemnon,” written in the 5th century BC.

Schliemann undoubtedly used the death mask to generate media interest in his excavations at the Bronze Age site, but it’s _extremely_ unlikely that it belonged to the Homeric hero, if indeed Agamemnon ever existed as a historical figure.

![Image 5](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Grave-Circle-A.jpg)

Scale model of Mycenae. Grave Circle A is located to the right after the Lion Gate, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel.

What we do know is that Schliemann, who retired from commercial activities a multi-millionaire at the age of 36, was **a fanatical devotee of Homer, dedicating the rest of his life to proving the historicity of the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_**. As such, he gained a reputation for “salting” his archaeological digs with bogus artifacts or objects taken from elsewhere to back up his claims.

His first quest took him to Hissarlik in northwest Turkey, in search of **the ancient citadel of Troy**. From 1870 to 1873, his excavations, inlcuding the discovery of **a large cache of gold artifacts dubbed “Priam’s Treasure,”** brought him both international fame and notoriety in equal measure, especially among the academic elite who criticised his heavy-handed methods.

In 1874, Schliemann embarked on excavations at Mycenae, the heavily fortified center that gives its name to **the Late Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece from c. 1600 to 1200 BC**. The discovery and subsequent publication of the spectacular contents of Grave Circle A, inlcuding the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon,” sparked a global media frenzy at the time, but not everyone was convinced.

Greek history books

Created from a single sheet of gold, heated and hammered against a wooden mold, **the mask differs in style from the other death masks of Mycenae**, lending support to the theory that Schliemann may have had it manufactured and surreptitiously placed in the shaft grave as part of an elaborate hoax. Proponents of this argument state that it is the only one in three-dimensional form as opposed to flat, with cut-out ears, a finely-detailed beard and handlebar moustache, conspicuously different to how men are depicted in Mycenaean art, and the eyebrows form two arches instead of one. It is also extremely well preserved compared to the others.

![Image 6](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Gold-Death-Mask.jpg)

One of the other funeral masks from Grave Circle A at Mycenae, also dated to the 16th century BC, but quite different in style to the so-called "Mask of Agamemnon."

So, was it just a publicity stunt? Did Schliemann really fabricate the mask? Or was he simply letting his imagination get the better of him?

Towards the end of this life, Schliemann, accepting doubts about the authenticity of the mask’s true owner, famously conceded: “So this is not Agamemnon … these are not his ornaments? All right, let’s call him Schulze.” But **he certainly made no admission of fraud**.

Instead, modern archaeological research has tentatively dated the mask to **the second half of the 16th century BC, at least 300 years _before_ the Trojan War** of _Iliad_-fame. One study even dated it as far back as 2500 BC – the Early Helladic period of mainland Greece.

The majority of scholars today agree that **the gold mask is authentically Mycenaean, an exquisite example of the early repoussé (embossing) technique**, and likely belonged to a warrior king or someone of extreme wealth and importance in early Mycenaean culture. Interestingly, death masks like the ones found at Mycenae have not been found at any other site from the Mycenaean world. As such, the mystery surrounding their origins continues.

The iconic “Mask of Agamemnon,” even if it didn’t belong to the Homeric king, is nevertheless an extraordinary treasure of prehistoric Greek archaeology. It can be seen **on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens**, mounted centrally with the other gold masks from Grave Circle A, amid the spectacular Collection of Mycenaean Antiquities.

Interestingly, death masks like the ones found at Mycenae have not been found at any other site from the Mycenaean world. As such, the mystery surrounding their origins continues.

The iconic “Mask of Agamemnon,” even if it didn’t belong to the Homeric king, is nevertheless an extraordinary treasure of prehistoric Greek archaeology. It can be seen **on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens**, mounted centrally with the other gold masks from Grave Circle A, amid the spectacular Collection of Mycenaean Antiquities.

**THE MYCENAEAN CIVILIZATION**

The Mycenaean world (1600-1100 BC) developed in Greece, which has always served as a bridge between the East and the West. Its impact stretched from Asia Minor, the Near East and Egypt to the Western Mediterranean and North-western Europe. It is traditionally believed that its bearers, the Greek-speaking Achaeans, settled in Greece in around 2000 BC. The inception of the Mycenaean civilization that was called after its largest centre, Mycenae in the Peloponnese, was marked by the rise of groups of warrior kings who maintained relations with the already advanced Minoan civilization of Crete. A vivid picture of the wealth of the early Mycenaean Period is unveiled in the royal shaft graves of Mycenae (Grave Circles A and B of Mycenae), dated to the 16th century BC, with the valuable grave goods, symbols of social status and office that formed the basis for Homer’s golden Mycenae.

The large palaces of Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos in the Peloponnese, as well as at Thebes in Boeotia, which were enclosed by strong Cyclopean walls, constituted administrative, economic, military and religious centres of the respective wider regions. The central administration, hierarchically organized, led by the “anax” (king), maintained archives that consisted of clay tablets inscribed with Linear B script, the first Greek script, adapted to the Greek language of the Minoan Linear A precursor. The acropolises were surrounded by organized settlements and cemeteries of chamber tombs whose opulent grave goods reveal social stratification and a prosperous society. The magnificent tholos (beehive) tombs, such as the tholos tomb of Atreus (Treasury of Atreus), the Vapheio tholos tomb at Laconia or the tholos tombs of mythical Iolkos in Thessaly were intended for the ruling elite.

According to tradition, the demise of the Mycenaean centralized palatial administration system took place in the late 13th century BC after the Trojan War which was a joint venture of the Achaean rulers. The causes can be traced in the social unrest, the economic decline and the migration of peoples “”of the land and the sea”” across the Mediterranean that destroyed the centres of Asia Minor and the East, and also in the archaeologically attested powerful earthquakes. These changes signalled the beginning of a new period in Greece during the 12th century BC which was the last century of the Mycenaean civilization. The new conditions favoured the unrestricted development of local centres in the Peloponnese, the Cyclades and Crete, whereas life continued in the known acropolises, at Mycenae and mainly Tiryns. The end of the Mycenaean civilization during the 11th century BC inevitably brought about a cultural decline; nevertheless, during the Geometric period and until the 8th century BC the way was paved for the emergence of the Greek city. The Mycenaean civilization has been consigned to myth and legend ever since.

**THE MYCENAEAN CIVILIZATION**

The Mycenaean world (1600-1100 BC) developed in Greece, which has always served as a bridge between the East and the West. Its impact stretched from Asia Minor, the Near East and Egypt to the Western Mediterranean and North-western Europe. It is traditionally believed that its bearers, the Greek-speaking Achaeans, settled in Greece in around 2000 BC. The inception of the Mycenaean civilization that was called after its largest centre, Mycenae in the Peloponnese, was marked by the rise of groups of warrior kings who maintained relations with the already advanced Minoan civilization of Crete. A vivid picture of the wealth of the early Mycenaean Period is unveiled in the royal shaft graves of Mycenae (Grave Circles A and B of Mycenae), dated to the 16th century BC, with the valuable grave goods, symbols of social status and office that formed the basis for Homer’s golden Mycenae.

The large palaces of Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos in the Peloponnese, as well as at Thebes in Boeotia, which were enclosed by strong Cyclopean walls, constituted administrative, economic, military and religious centres of the respective wider regions. The central administration, hierarchically organized, led by the “anax” (king), maintained archives that consisted of clay tablets inscribed with Linear B script, the first Greek script, adapted to the Greek language of the Minoan Linear A precursor. The acropolises were surrounded by organized settlements and cemeteries of chamber tombs whose opulent grave goods reveal social stratification and a prosperous society. The magnificent tholos (beehive) tombs, such as the tholos tomb of Atreus (Treasury of Atreus), the Vapheio tholos tomb at Laconia or the tholos tombs of mythical Iolkos in Thessaly were intended for the ruling elite.

According to tradition, the demise of the Mycenaean centralized palatial administration system took place in the late 13th century BC after the Trojan War which was a joint venture of the Achaean rulers. The causes can be traced in the social unrest, the economic decline and the migration of peoples “”of the land and the sea”” across the Mediterranean that destroyed the centres of Asia Minor and the East, and also in the archaeologically attested powerful earthquakes. These changes signalled the beginning of a new period in Greece during the 12th century BC which was the last century of the Mycenaean civilization. The new conditions favoured the unrestricted development of local centres in the Peloponnese, the Cyclades and Crete, whereas life continued in the known acropolises, at Mycenae and mainly Tiryns. The end of the Mycenaean civilization during the 11th century BC inevitably brought about a cultural decline; nevertheless, during the Geometric period and until the 8th century BC the way was paved for the emergence of the Greek city. The Mycenaean civilization has been consigned to myth and legend ever since.

![Image 5](https://www.namuseum.gr/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/IMG_2691_gallery-1920x988.jpg)

The Mycenaean world (1600-1100 BC) developed in Greece, which has always served as a bridge between the East and the West. Its impact stretched from Asia Minor, the Near East and Egypt to the Western Mediterranean and North-western Europe. It is traditionally believed that its bearers, the Greek-speaking Achaeans, settled in Greece in around 2000 BC. The inception of the Mycenaean civilization that was called after its largest centre, Mycenae in the Peloponnese, was marked by the rise of groups of warrior kings who maintained relations with the already advanced Minoan civilization of Crete. A vivid picture of the wealth of the early Mycenaean Period is unveiled in the royal shaft graves of Mycenae (Grave Circles A and B of Mycenae), dated to the 16th century BC, with the valuable grave goods, symbols of social status and office that formed the basis for Homer’s golden Mycenae.

The large palaces of Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos in the Peloponnese, as well as at Thebes in Boeotia, which were enclosed by strong Cyclopean walls, constituted administrative, economic, military and religious centres of the respective wider regions. The central administration, hierarchically organized, led by the “anax” (king), maintained archives that consisted of clay tablets inscribed with Linear B script, the first Greek script, adapted to the Greek language of the Minoan Linear A precursor. The acropolises were surrounded by organized settlements and cemeteries of chamber tombs whose opulent grave goods reveal social stratification and a prosperous society. The magnificent tholos (beehive) tombs, such as the tholos tomb of Atreus (Treasury of Atreus), the Vapheio tholos tomb at Laconia or the tholos tombs of mythical Iolkos in Thessaly were intended for the ruling elite.

According to tradition, the demise of the Mycenaean centralized palatial administration system took place in the late 13th century BC after the Trojan War which was a joint venture of the Achaean rulers. The causes can be traced in the social unrest, the economic decline and the migration of peoples “of the land and the sea” across the Mediterranean that destroyed the centres of Asia Minor and the East, and also in the archaeologically attested powerful earthquakes. These changes signalled the beginning of the new period in Greece during the 12th century BC which was the last century of the Mycenaean civilization. The new conditions favoured the unrestricted development of local centres in the Peloponnese, the Cyclades and Crete, whereas life continued in the known acropolises, at Mycenae and mainly Tiryns. The end of the Mycenaean civilization during the 11th century BC inevitably brought about a cultural decline; nevertheless, during the Geometric period and until the 8th century BC the way was paved for the emergence of the Greek city. The Mycenaean civilization has been consigned to myth and legend ever since.

**Room 4**  
 Room 4 introduces us to the radiance of the Mycenaean gold. The glorious Mycenaean civilization is presented in three units. Guardians and at the same time heralds of its reputation, the imposing grave stelae stand at the entrance of the exhibition. The valuable tableware and ritual vessels, the daggers with the impressed decoration, the masterful signet rings, the exotic artefacts as well as the large number of bronze weapons of the deceased rulers comprise the first unit of the exhibition. Centrally mounted are the watchful gold death masks, emblems of the first great civilization of Mainland Greece.

The second unit of the exhibition discloses the secrets of the Mycenaean palaces. In the thematically arranged display cases visitors are acquainted with the religious life of the major centres, the palatial art of wall paintings, the production of the royal workshops, the state archives written in Linear B, the international relations and the overseas trade of the great centres of the Peloponnese. The “Warrior Stele” and the “Warrior Vase” in the centre praise the military preparedness of the acropolises, whereas the exquisite “Ivory Triad” is revealing of the charm of the peaceful religious life.

The exhibits of the final unit focus on the world of the dead. The relief half-columns that come from the entrance of the “Treasury of Atreus” serve as the setting for the display of a selection of gold, silver, stone and clay vessels, jewels made of gold, glass paste and faience used as grave goods of the deceased of the city of Mycenae and the royal tombs at Dendra. The centre is dominated by the superb cups and other treasures that had been deposited in the tholos (beehive) tombs at Vapheio in Laconia, at Myrsinochori and Pylos, the other major Mycenaean centres of the Peloponnese.

**Room 3**The Small Mycenaean Room (Room 3) is dedicated to the life and the accomplishments of the Mycenaean centres outside the Peloponnese. A complete picture of Mycenaean Attica is uniquely offered with selections of the wonderful creations made of ivory and the glass artefacts from the tombs of Menidi and Spata, curious ritual vessels of Attica made of clay and the finds from the Acropolis of Athens, grave goods from tombs at Mesogaia or the coast, groups typical of the final phases of the Mycenaean Period from Perati and others from Salamis. The gold grave goods from the tholos (beehive) tombs of N. Ionia (Kapakli) and Dimini at Volos and also the ensembles from Kythera and Skopelos are revealing of the wealth of the regional areas.

At the far end of the Room, set in the large display case that presents the development of pottery, a selection of clay vases has been made, with shape and decoration typical of the time period, that characterize the aesthetic taste of everyday life and date the phases of the Mycenaean Period.
